strengths: GHOST presents a clear and potentially useful idea: optimize a surrogate visual embedding using target-model feedback and decode it through diffusion, avoiding backpropagation through the full generation pipeline.
The study covers three source MLLMs, including a reasoning model, and several transfer targets; the reported generation scale and attack success rates are substantial.
The paper combines quantitative evaluation, qualitative examples, human judgments, hyperparameter studies, and a proof-of-concept mitigation experiment.
The generated images are generally natural-looking, and the appendix provides useful implementation details, class-wise results, prompts, and mapper evaluations.
weaknesses: The central causal claim lacks a crucial baseline: the paper does not report hallucination rates for ordinary unCLIP reconstructions produced from the same selected inputs without embedding optimization. Thus, it is unclear how much success comes from GHOST rather than diffusion artifacts or regeneration alone.

The transferability results are seriously confounded because original images are screened only against the source model. No target-model performance on the corresponding original or unoptimized images is reported, so the high cross-model rates may partly reflect pre-existing hallucinations induced by the CLIP-selected contexts.

Whether successful images truly lack the target object is ambiguous. Success is primarily certified by one detector, while humans report seeing the object in 11.0–13.7% of evaluated GHOST images. Several qualitative examples deliberately introduce strongly object-like shapes, blurring the distinction between hallucination and legitimate recognition of ambiguous visual content.

The human study does not report per-image consensus, inter-annotator agreement, uncertainty, participant assignment, or a decision rule for declaring an image object-free. Aggregate votes therefore cannot validate each of the thousands of claimed successes.

The DASH comparison is not well controlled: DASH has a different retrieval-oriented objective, is evaluated outside its intended ReLAION setup, uses a much larger and structurally different input pool, and one important variant could not be run for LLaVA. Raw counts and success percentages are consequently not directly comparable.

FID is a weak measure of perceptual similarity and object absence, and some reported realism results are worse for GHOST. No paired perceptual metric, reconstruction baseline, distortion distribution, or blinded preference study establishes that edits are consistently minimal while preserving semantics.

The ablations do not isolate all core components. In particular, there is no end-to-end comparison without the adversarial loss, mapper, CLIP penalty, partial-noising strategy, or prompt randomization under otherwise identical conditions.

The mitigation experiment is under-specified and potentially affected by model-selection leakage: the number and class composition of training images are omitted, POPE training-split performance selects checkpoints, and results lack repeated runs, uncertainty, and stronger mitigation baselines.

Reproducibility is incomplete: mapper training data size and splits, diffusion checkpoint details, random seeds, runtime and compute costs, API/model versions for closed models, and code or artifact availability are not adequately documented.
The paper does not discuss dual-use risks or release safeguards for a method explicitly designed to generate transferable adversarial inputs against closed and open multimodal systems.

strengths: GHOST presents a relevant and intuitive stress-testing idea: optimize a surrogate visual embedding using feedback from the victim MLLM, then decode it into a natural image with an image-conditioned diffusion model.

The learned mapper decouples optimization from diffusion generation, potentially making the approach more modular and computationally practical than end-to-end differentiation through the complete pipeline.
The empirical study has useful breadth, covering three source MLLMs, ten object classes, cross-model evaluation, human judgments, several ablations, and a proof-of-concept mitigation experiment.
The generated examples demonstrate that contextual or shape-based cues can alter model predictions, and the reported attack rates indicate an important robustness problem worth studying.
weaknesses: The central success metric does not reliably establish hallucination. A sample is counted when OWLv2 fails to detect the target, but detector false negatives do not prove object absence—especially for small, distorted, or partially formed objects deliberately produced by the method. Human evaluation still labels the target present in 11.0% and 13.7% of the two evaluated sets, so a material fraction of reported successes are not hallucinations by the paper's own evidence.

The human study is insufficient to repair this validity problem. It evaluates only subsets, uses binary answers without an ambiguity option, obtains only a few judgments per image on average, recruits unspecified peers, and reports no confidence intervals or inter-annotator agreement. The control accuracy is only 91.2%.

The transferability results do not appear to compare each edited image against its corresponding original on every target model. Images are filtered for non-hallucination only on the source model; a target model may already answer yes on the original. Consequently, rates such as 66.5% for GPT-4o cannot be interpreted as GHOST-induced transfer without paired flip rates or baseline-adjusted effects.

The comparison with DASH is not controlled. DASH has a different retrieval-oriented objective, originally operates over ReLAION-5B, and is evaluated here on COCO under a modified setting. Comparing raw discoveries from 9,423 inputs with those from 118,000 differently processed candidates does not substantiate the claimed orders-of-magnitude methodological advantage. Runtime, GPU cost, number of generations, and total model-query budgets are also missing despite efficiency being a key claim.

Image-quality evidence is weak. FID is a distributional metric and is not an appropriate measure of paired semantic fidelity to original images; uncertainty and sample counts are not reported. GHOST is also worse than the baselines on every reported realism FID, substantially so for GLM, which conflicts with the strong naturalness claims.

The mitigation experiment is explicitly a small toy study and omits essential details such as training-set size and class composition. Model selection uses POPE, the positive synthetic samples are not rigorously validated, and evaluation on two attack-generated sets plus limited general-task checks is inadequate to support the claim that GHOST is a corrective tool rather than teaching a narrow rejection heuristic.

Several claims exceed the evidence: the mapper retains only 54.5% relative semantic score for LLaVA, the unsorted-input experiment changes both diffusion noise and the confidence threshold and therefore does not isolate sorting, and most ablations cover only two to four classes. There is also no substantive limitations, misuse, or ethical discussion for a method explicitly designed to generate adversarial images.

strengths: GHOST is a clear and practically meaningful contribution: it turns object-hallucination evaluation from a fixed-benchmark exercise into targeted, model-informed stress testing through embedding optimization and diffusion-based image generation.

The decoupled mapper-based design is technically interesting and substantially more scalable than differentiating through the full MLLM–diffusion pipeline. The paper supplies mapper evaluations, attack hyperparameters, prompt templates, and component ablations.

The empirical scope is strong. Results cover three source MLLMs, including a reasoning model, ten object classes, thousands of successful cases, and transfer to several open- and closed-source models. The high cross-model transfer rates are especially noteworthy.

The authors evaluate object absence and image quality through complementary mechanisms: detector filtering, human judgments from 40 participants, FID-based comparisons, and qualitative examples. Human judgments indicate that most generated images remain object-free.

The mitigation experiment is a useful proof of concept: fine-tuning substantially reduces hallucination on GHOST images from unseen source models, improves POPE, and leaves VQAv2 and captioning performance approximately unchanged.
weaknesses: The transferability experiment lacks a crucial control: each target model should also be evaluated on the corresponding original images. Because seeds are deliberately selected for high CLIP similarity to the target object, some reported cross-model hallucinations may be pre-existing target-model failures rather than effects transferred from GHOST edits.

The headline success rates rely on OWLv2 as the decisive object-absence filter, although human evaluation finds the target object present in 11.0% and 13.7% of evaluated LLaVA and Qwen images. The binary annotation protocol also provides no ambiguity option, and GLM images receive no reported human validation. Human-validated or uncertainty-adjusted success rates would better support the central quantitative claim.

The comparison with DASH is not fully controlled. GHOST and DASH use different search mechanisms, generation budgets, candidate-selection procedures, and original objectives; reporting discovered-image counts without matched compute, runtime, or query budgets weakens the orders-of-magnitude efficiency claim.

Image-quality evidence is incomplete. FID is a distribution-level metric and does not directly establish per-image realism or minimality of edits; GHOST is also worse than baselines on several realism comparisons, particularly for GLM. LPIPS or perceptual-distance measurements, blinded realism ratings, and evaluation on equally sized matched sets would be more convincing.

Several reproducibility details are missing or underspecified, including the mapper training dataset size and split, exact fine-tuning-set size and class composition, random-seed variability, computational cost, and a code/data release statement. The fine-tuning study is explicitly small-scale and uses checkpoint selection on POPE, so its broader mitigation conclusion remains preliminary.

strengths: The paper addresses an important reliability problem with a clear and interesting method: a learned mapper enables efficient optimization using MLLM feedback while decoupling the diffusion model from the optimization loop.
The empirical study is substantial, covering three victim MLLMs, ten object classes, a reasoning model, an additional dataset, cross-model transfer, and a mitigation experiment.

The authors make meaningful efforts to verify object absence and image quality through human judgments, multiple object detectors, FID, SSIM, and naturalness ratings. The conservative detector ensemble still yields a 22.7% success rate.

weaknesses: The central causal comparison is missing: the paper does not report hallucination rates when the same inputs are passed through unCLIP using their original, unoptimized embeddings under the same four-attempt budget. Consequently, it is unclear how much of the reported 28–32% success comes from GHOST optimization rather than stochastic diffusion reconstruction itself.

The comparison with DASH is not sufficiently controlled. DASH is adapted to a different dataset and search regime, and its goal is retrieval of naturally occurring failures rather than synthesis from each input. Comparing discovered-image counts or rates over very different pools does not establish the claimed orders-of-magnitude advantage. Stronger matched baselines, including unoptimized unCLIP and prompt-based generation, are needed.

The transferability analysis does not report whether each target model already hallucinated on the corresponding original image. Since inputs are selected only to be negatives for the source model and are deliberately chosen for high CLIP similarity to the target object, the 66.5% GPT-4o result may substantially include pre-existing target-model errors rather than vulnerabilities transferred by GHOST. Per-model original-image baselines and paired flip rates are essential.

The mitigation evaluation has test-set leakage: the authors state that configurations are selected using POPE, then report performance on POPE. It also uses one model and apparently one seed, without a matched synthetic-data baseline, validation split, uncertainty estimates, or evaluation on held-out GHOST attacks. Thus the corrective-tool claim is preliminary.

Several validation studies are too limited for the breadth of the claims. Naturalness is assessed on only 30 GHOST images; human object-absence evaluation excludes GLM and ObjectNet; and the attribute/relation extension has no detector or human verification that generation did not actually make the queried predicate true. Some qualitative attribute/relation examples appear compatible with genuine predicate insertion.

Important ablations are absent, including full removal of each objective term, a comparison without the mapper-guided optimization, and matched generation-budget controls. Mapper training data size and split are also unspecified, while its reported reconstruction accuracy is only moderate.

The claim that GHOST requires “no prior knowledge” is overstated: optimization requires white-box gradients and a separately trained model-specific mapper, while evaluation relies on target labels, dataset annotations, and object detectors. Closed models are assessed only through transfer.

The experiments cover three source MLLMs, several transfer targets, two image datasets, a reasoning model, detector-ensemble filtering, human evaluation, runtime, and a preliminary mitigation study.

The reported attack yield and cross-model transfer rates are potentially significant, while the qualitative examples illustrate semantically meaningful failure cases rather than imperceptible pixel perturbations.
The appendix provides many implementation details, including prompts, hyperparameters, class-level counts, mapper evaluation, and fine-tuning settings.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is inadequately controlled: the paper never reports hallucination rates for matched unCLIP reconstructions generated from the original, unoptimized embeddings with the same noise level, number of attempts, filtering, and selected inputs. Diffusion reconstruction alone could introduce object-like cues or cause prediction flips, so the reported success rate cannot be cleanly attributed to GHOST's optimization.

The headline comparison with DASH is not apples-to-apples. DASH is designed to retrieve naturally occurring failures from a web-scale corpus, whereas GHOST synthesizes several candidates per selected COCO input. The reproduction changes DASH's intended data regime because its private ReLAION search infrastructure was unavailable, yet the paper emphasizes orders-of-magnitude superiority using incomparable denominators and objectives.

Absence of the target object is not established reliably for the full evaluation. Main results rely on one detector, and humans judge only subsets for Qwen and LLaVA—not GLM, ObjectNet, or transfer experiments. Moreover, 11.0% and 13.7% of human judgments say the target is present, which is substantial for samples counted as hallucinations. The four-detector experiment is limited to five classes and still cannot rule out shared detector failures.

The transferability claim lacks essential controls: rates are measured on source-selected successful images without reporting target-model responses to the corresponding originals or matched unoptimized diffusion outputs. Consequently, the very high GPT-4o and other transfer rates may reflect selection bias, genuinely object-like generated content, or generic diffusion-induced cues rather than shared model vulnerabilities.

There is no convincing end-to-end ablation isolating the adversarial objective. The paper varies individual hyperparameters but does not compare against random embedding perturbations, optimization without the adversarial loss, direct CLIP-object steering, or an untrained/alternative mapper under the complete success criterion.

Mapper training is insufficiently specified: the dataset, its size, and separation from evaluation images are unclear. The mapper also preserves semantics imperfectly—reported relative scores fall to 54.5% for LLaVA—raising concern that optimization exploits surrogate reconstruction errors. No uncertainty or variability across mapper training runs is reported.

The mitigation evidence is weak and potentially biased. Multiple fine-tuning configurations are selected using POPE and then performance on POPE is reported, apparently without a separate validation split. The positive synthetic labels are not independently verified, and the study uses one model, one seed, a small dataset, and no comparison against equally sized generic or non-adversarial synthetic training data.

Image-quality evidence is limited. FID is a distribution-level metric and does not verify object absence or perceptual validity of individual attacks; sample counts and uncertainty are not reported. The naturalness study uses only 30 images per condition, provides no statistical test or confidence intervals, and relies on an unspecified peer population.

Overall, the idea is promising and the experimental breadth is notable, but missing matched generation controls and weaknesses in ground-truth validation undermine the main effectiveness and transfer claims. These are central evaluation issues rather than minor omissions, making the submission insufficiently supported for a top-tier venue in its current form.

strengths: GHOST presents a clear and meaningful contribution: it actively synthesizes natural-looking inputs that expose model-specific object hallucinations, rather than being limited to a fixed benchmark.

The decoupled design—learning a mapper from CLIP embeddings to MLLM visual tokens, optimizing in embedding space, and decoding with unCLIP—is technically interesting and substantially more efficient than an end-to-end diffusion optimization loop.

The empirical scope is strong: three source MLLMs, ten COCO categories, an ObjectNet evaluation, transfer to several open and closed models, human evaluation, image-quality measurements, hyperparameter studies, and a mitigation experiment.

The reported attack yield is substantial and consistent across source models (28.1–32.4%), and the conservative four-detector experiment still obtains a 22.7% success rate. Cross-model transfer further suggests that the method uncovers shared visual failure modes rather than only source-model artifacts.

Human judgments and SSIM results provide useful evidence that many generated images remain object-free, natural, and structurally close to their inputs. The LoRA experiment also gives promising evidence that discovered failures can support mitigation.
The paper is well motivated, clearly organized, visually persuasive, and supplies extensive implementation details and supplementary code.
weaknesses: The central claim that successful images do not contain the target object is not fully established at the reported scale. The main success counts rely on one detector, while humans judged the object present in 11.0–13.7% of sampled GHOST images. Results are reported as aggregate votes rather than per-image consensus, with no inter-annotator agreement or uncertainty estimates, and GLM-generated images are not covered by the human study.

The headline comparison with DASH is not fully controlled. DASH is designed around retrieval from a web-scale corpus, is evaluated here on COCO because its intended retrieval service is unavailable, and receives a much larger but structurally different candidate pool. GHOST also generates up to four candidates per input. Accordingly, the orders-of-magnitude comparison in successful counts should be interpreted cautiously.

Transferability rates are measured on images already selected for successfully attacking the source model, but the paper does not report matched baselines for ordinary unCLIP reconstructions, original images, or non-optimized edits on the same target models. Without these controls, the fraction of transfer attributable specifically to GHOST optimization is unclear.

Several evaluations lack statistical reporting or sufficiently controlled comparisons. There are no confidence intervals or repeated-run variability; main FID comparisons may involve differently selected or sized sample sets; and the mitigation model is selected on POPE and then evaluated on POPE, without a held-out model-selection split or multiple training seeds.

The mapper preserves only 54.5% relative semantic score for LLaVA under the paper's GPT-4-based evaluation, yet there is no ablation comparing the learned mapper against alternative alignment mechanisms or quantifying how mapper error affects attack selection. Key component ablations are also incomplete: the paper does not cleanly remove each of Ladv, Lclip, and Lreg and report both valid attack rate and image quality.

The extension to attribute and relation hallucinations is preliminary and lacks human verification or an automated ground-truth check. There are also reproducibility ambiguities, including the counterintuitive and insufficiently explained diffusion-noise convention in Appendix F.1 and minor notation inconsistencies in the compositional CLIP embedding definition.

The work enables targeted attacks on deployed multimodal systems, but the manuscript does not provide a dedicated ethical or misuse discussion. Overall, the contribution is competitive and leans toward acceptance, but the evidence does not yet support an unqualified Accept score.
